source.title: K-SAM: Sharpness-Aware Minimization at the Speed of SGD
source.authors: Renkun Ni; Ping-Yeh Chiang; Jonas Geiping; Micah Goldblum; A. Wilson; T. Goldstein

record.tranche_reason: The study reports results on sharpness-aware optimization, gradient approximations, and benchmark accuracy, but does not test the claim versions about memorization of random labels, width past interpolation, convolutional inductive bias, optimizer comparisons, large-batch gaps, dropout, generalization measures, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: K-SAM/SAM accuracy comparisons and gradient-alignment measurements concern optimizer performance and approximation fidelity. They do not measure the train-test generalization gap or any listed version. Reported prior-work claims are citations, not this study's own results.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization rationale to develop an efficient SAM optimizer and reports benchmark accuracy, runtime, memory, and gradient alignment. It does not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking of train–test gaps. Its other experiments do not test V1–V6 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: top-loss subsets approximate SAM's ascent and descent gradients and substantially reduce computation while often preserving benchmark performance. The text qualifies this conclusion on ImageNet, where small subsets reduce accuracy and preserving SAM-level accuracy requires more computation than SGD.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces K-SAM, a top-loss-subset variant of SAM, and evaluates it against SGD, SAM, and ESAM; it does not reproduce the original study methods represented by the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: K-SAM performance and efficiency vary with dataset, subset sizes K1 and K2, and whether the task is ImageNet versus CIFAR or GLUE; small subsets particularly reduce ImageNet accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: K-SAM approximates SAM gradients using high-loss subsets and often approaches SAM's held-out accuracy with less computation; ImageNet requires larger subsets to preserve accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-loss gradient subsampling can reduce SAM's computational cost while approximately preserving its benchmark performance, with task-dependent accuracy–cost trade-offs.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 reports cosine alignment between subset and full-batch gradients; Figure 2 finds weaker alignment on ImageNet, especially with small subsets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-loss subsets approximate full-batch gradient directions better than random subsets in the tested settings.

record.problems: The study reports benchmark test accuracy and gradient alignment, not training error, test error gaps, random-label fitting, or the mapped properties in the claim. Its experiments therefore do not establish or challenge the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: reported experimental outcomes concern K-SAM/SAM benchmark accuracy, runtime, memory, and gradient alignment, none of which measure the claim versions' named behaviors or properties.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization with the same architectures and training recipes.
Test-error changes as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; SAM and K-SAM are not adaptive gradient methods of the kind this version names.
Large versus small training batches under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations. Subsampling gradients within a fixed batch does not establish this comparison.
Controlled dropout comparisons and their dependence on dataset size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with train–test gaps at comparable training loss, and its ranking relative to norm and margin measures.
Retraining after removing examples selected by memorization influence versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No result rows require correction. The omitted optimizer-performance and gradient-alignment results are declared in rows_left_out. Accuracy gains from a sharpness-aware optimizer alone do not establish V7's specific correlation between magnitude-aware sharpness and generalization gaps.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local-connectivity effects.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning regimes, and optimizer-dependent generalization.
Large versus small batch effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to train-test gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
